claims.text: As-quenched 316L-type Cr-bearing stainless steel has a random solid-solution microstructure in both its bulk and near-surface regions.
Aging at 650°C for 10 hours followed by controlled cooling enhances local chemical ordering in Cr-bearing stainless steel.
The ordering induced by the proposed bulk thermal treatment is confined primarily to the near-surface region.
Thermal aging promotes preferential Cr and Ni segregation near the surface.
Preferential Cr and Ni segregation produces a more coherent, uniform, crack-free, and defect-minimized passive oxide film.
Near-surface chemical ordering restricts atomic mobility.
Local ordering by Cr and Ni clustering reduces compositional fluctuations.
The ordered near-surface structure suppresses the formation of micro-galvanic cells.
Suppressing micro-galvanic cells enables formation of a continuously protective passive film.
The uniform passive film limits pitting corrosion under harsh chemical and elevated-temperature conditions.
Relative to as-quenched specimens, LCO-enhanced specimens will have lower corrosion current density.
Relative to as-quenched specimens, LCO-enhanced specimens will have a lower density of corrosion pits.
Relative to as-quenched specimens, LCO-enhanced specimens will develop a more homogeneous and crack-free passive film.
Untreated as-quenched stainless steel exhibits heterogeneous passive-film formation.
Untreated as-quenched stainless steel has higher corrosion current density and more frequent pitting than the proposed aged state under identical exposure conditions.
Corrected TEM and diffraction analysis can resolve the size and distribution of local chemical order.
The proposed mechanism should hold in 3.5 wt.% NaCl and pH approximately 3 aqueous media between room temperature and about 90°C.
Exposure at about 90°C in the selected media simulates relevant chemical-processing and nuclear-power operating conditions.
